Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Review the history of workers’ compensation.
Measure the unique aspects of caring for a patient under a work claim.
Apply terminology used in workers’ compensation and discern how it differs from use in other
contexts.
Distinguish science/knowledge from law, policy, and precedent.
Practice recording and documenting facts, stating best evidence and noting and documenting
unexpected symptom intensity and incapability.
Distinguish risk-based restrictions (activities that may cause new pathophysiology or that put
others at risk), incapacity (activities that are not possible because of pathology [impairment]),

and activity intolerance (an individual’s sense of what they are willing or unwilling to do).
Differentiate activity intolerance caused by incapacity from activity intolerance related to
stress, distress, and misconceptions.
Compose clear documentation regarding any incongruence between activity intolerance and
incapacity.
Determine that policy, law, and precedent may result in legal concepts and actions contrary to
best evidence and that physicians should always adhere to the science.
History
Compensation for work injuries began in the 1800s in Germany.1
During the industrial revolution, many workers were being harmed or killed in factories and
particularly in the railroad industry.
In the United States in the early 1900s, no federal workers’ compensation program existed;
therefore, each state legislated and developed its own program.
Workers’ compensation is a no-fault system in which employees do not have to prove legal
negligence on the part of the employer, and paid medical care and wage replacement benefits
are available promptly after injury.

History
Before workers’ compensation legislation instituting rules and regulations in the early
1900s, injured employees in the United States had to file a lawsuit and prove their
employer was negligent to receive lost wages and medical treatment coverage. The
workers’ compensation system that was developed was the grand bargain to replace this
contentious and cumbersome system. Work injury was made a no-fault system with
guaranteed benefits. The new system legally eliminated the three defenses that were
available to employers sued by workers for negligence: contributory negligence,
assumption of risk, and fellow servant rule. In 1902, Maryland was the first state in the
United States to adopt a workers’ compensation insurance program. By 1948, each state
had adopted its own workers’ compensation insurance program. Each state has its own
system for resolving employee-employer disputes, either medical or administrative.
Hawaii and Alaska included workers’ compensation legislation at the time they achieved
statehood. Indemnity payments, including partial payment of an employee’s usual
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:01 AM
AAOS | Workers’ Compensation
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001158
2/26

regular wage during recovery and a final award for the effect of permanent objective
impairment of the body part that was injured to reflect decreased earning capacity, are
typical parts of the system.
In addition, federal workers’ compensation acts cover federal employees and some other
groups. These acts include the Federal Employees’ Compensation Act, which covers
federal employees; the Federal Employers’ Liability Act, which covers railroad workers;
the Longshore and Harbor Workers’ Compensation Act; and the Defense Base Act, which
covers civilian workers at overseas US military bases. Other programs cover specific
subsets of employees, including the Energy Employees Occupational Illness
Compensation Program and the Black Lung Program.
Current System
Workers’ compensation obligates an employer to
Compensate the injured worker for high-quality, timely care of a work injury
Pay a percentage of wages for a specific duration (the percentage and duration vary from
state to state)
Pay a final settlement based on permanent impairment related to the injury.
A workers’ compensation program benefits the employer by
Shielding the employer from being sued for negligence, except in egregious circumstances
Precluding claims against the employer for pain and suffering, emotional distress, punitive
damages, and bad faith.
Initiation of a Work Claim
The employee, employer, and/or or the medical care provider is required to timely report a
work injury and use workers’ compensation insurance.
The employer must report the injury to the insurance carrier of record and the Occupational
Safety and Health Administration and the state agency for workers’ compensation.
The insurance carrier assigns an adjuster to help navigate the worker to the resolution of the
claim.
The adjuster promptly determines whether the insurance company will accept or deny the
claim.


Initiation of a Work Claim
Even if an employee has regular health insurance, it is not applicable to the work injury
and cannot be used. The employee must report the injury to his or her supervisor or
safety manager or directly to the employer. The employer has a duty to report the injury
to the insurance carrier of record, Occupational Safety and Health Administration, and
the respective state agency for workers’ compensation. Only the most minor of injuries
need not be reported to the federal government in the Occupational Safety and Health
Administration log. An orthopaedic specialist does not have to keep special records and
data for reporting issues. The treating doctor of record—orthopaedic surgeon, family
practice physician, or occupational medicine physician—must keep appropriate clinical
records and documentation in the medical record. The tasks of reporting and
documenting the existence of a claim to the correct state or federal agency fall to the
employer and the insurance carrier.
An insurance adjuster is assigned to the claim. It is the adjuster’s responsibility to ensure
that the claim progresses to resolution. The simplest of claims are termed medical only.
These injuries do not result in any lost time from work. The assigned adjuster may or
may not stay with the claim for its term. With a more severe claim or if new body parts or
diagnoses are added, other adjusters with more specialized training may take over
management of the claim. Claims that become more complex and result in lost time
from work are known as indemnity claims.
The adjuster/carrier has a certain number of days in which to investigate the claim
specifics and accept or deny the claim in part or total. An investigation occurs with every
claim, and the time requirements vary by state. A workers’ compensation claim
investigation is a time-consuming effort and requires the participation of all
stakeholders, including the employee who is injured. An employee interview is
conducted via phone to gather the facts about the injury. The employer is interrogated
regarding its knowledge about the incident, including whether the incident was
witnessed or possibly videotaped. The medical records from the initial treating physician

all the way to the consulting specialists are reviewed for internal consistency and to
determine if the appropriate diagnosis is an injury as claimed.
Duties of the Orthopaedic Surgeon
Professional opinions should be based upon the best current scientific evidence.
Cognitive biases and cognitive errors are common. People (patients and clinicians) often
misinterpret aspects of illness. This is part of the normal function of the human mind.
Therefore, such misinterpretation should be anticipated and ameliorated with appropriate
debiasing strategies.
Society depends on musculoskeletal specialists to discern speculation, opinion, and a patient’s
subjective experience from the medical facts based on measurable pathophysiology.
Law, policy, and precedent can result in concepts and actions that may be inconsistent with
the best medical evidence. For example, conditions that are not caused by work may be
covered under workers’ compensation. Do not let these aspects of a work claim alter
adherence to current best evidence.
As a treating physician, your duties will include providing your learned medical opinion
regarding the following factors:
The cause of the injury
What part is new pathology from a work event (injury) and what part was already existing?
To what degree is the condition or are the new symptoms from existing pathology (eg, knee
arthritis or rotator cuff tendinopathy) rather than new pathology (injury)?
To what degree is the condition characterized by symptoms with no measurable pathology?
Are the symptoms out of proportion to the objective pathology?
The extent of the injury
What is the degree of new pathology?
The most likely course of management
What treatment options are required?
What treatment options are discretionary?
What are the options and the potential advantages and disadvantages of each?
Resolution of the injury
Timeline until medical restrictions are no longer appropriate (eg, healed fracture)?
What will the final permanent pathophysiology and impairment be?

5/26

Apportionment: What part of the permanent pathophysiology/impairment is from the
current work injury, what part is from a past work injury, and what part is not a result of
work injury (eg, arthritis, tendinopathy, prior injury)?
Some states apportion causation and other states do not.
In states that do not apportion causation, if an injury makes a pathology worse, the
employer is considered to have caused the entire pathology.
Work ability guidelines3,4
Surgeons are only responsible for medical restrictions and work capacity.
Restrictions: Tasks that are not safe to do because they will cause new pathology (eg,
heavy lifting before a fracture is healed that causes loss of fracture fragment reduction).
In other words, these are activities that are risky. Risk to coworkers also is considered.
Capacity: Tasks that cannot be performed because of objective impairment (eg, raising
the hand above the shoulder to work a piece of equipment if the shoulder has
permanently impaired motion). Capacity is objective and measurable pathophysiology. Do
not confuse capacity with symptoms or self-reported activity limitations (activity
intolerance), which are subjective.
Activity intolerance: Tasks that a patient reports they cannot perform but that should be
possible with the given pathophysiology and impairment. Activity intolerance is subjective
and reported by the patient.
Do not let activity tolerance influence your expertise regarding restrictions and capacity.
Keep these separate.
You can mention the activity intolerance, but do not confuse it with restrictions (risk) or
capacity. For example, restrictions are lifted after a fracture, sprain, or strain is healed to a
point at which the body is structurally sound, even if the patient has notable activity
intolerance.

Duties of the Orthopaedic Surgeon
An improved understanding of the forces necessary to produce specific types of injuries
is essential. This new evidence should supersede previous training and tradition, which
often was based on little or no scientific basis. Because it was the way we were taught is
no longer sufficient basis for your opinion. A good resource for best current medical
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:01 AM
AAOS | Workers’ Compensation
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001158
6/26

evidence is the American Medical Association’s AMA Guides to the Evaluation of Disease
and Injury Causation.2
Society depends on the musculoskeletal specialist to be forthright about age-related
changes, such as knee arthritis and rotator cuff tendinopathy; transient enthesopathies
of middle age that cannot be clearly ascribed to a work activity (eg, lateral epicondylitis
and plantar fasciitis), and tendinopathies and neuropathies evidence suggests are very
common, likely genetically mediated, and not experimentally linked to activity (eg, carpal
and cubital tunnel syndrome, trigger digit, de Quervain tendinopathy). Therefore,
orthopaedic surgeons do not require knowledge of what is approved for compensation
in their state. They can interpret the circumstance in terms of current best evidence. An
orthopaedic surgeon’s scientific opinion may be correct but may be rejected by a
workers’ compensation judge based on precedent (case law). Do not change your
scientific opinion to fit this legal opinion. The laws may eventually change.
The Biopsychosocial Paradigm of Illness
Lack of correspondence between activity tolerance and pathophysiology (impairment)
primarily results from social and mental factors.5
Stress: financial, home, job, relationship, role, or food insecurity, among others
Distress: symptoms of anxiety or depression
Misconceptions: worst-case thinking, fear of painful movement, or intolerance of uncertainty
Psychological distress is common among individuals seeking care for a work claim. Early
recognition and appropriate referral is important.
Individuals who are less able to talk about stress or distress occasionally communicate it via
physical manifestations, or somatization. Symptoms of somatization include specific
sensations, such as pain or chest tightness, and general fatigue or weakness. For example, in
English, the idiom “my boss is a pain in the neck” means my boss’s behavior makes my neck
hurt.
Factitious disorder is if patients assume a sick role by producing their disease. Examples
include individuals who traumatize the back of their hand (Secretan disorder), create edema
with a constriction band (factitious lymphedema), or seek multiple surgical procedures. The
most well-known factitious disorder is Munchausen syndrome.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:01 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001158
7/26

Malingering—accentuating or exaggerating an illness—is no longer considered a distinct
psychological diagnosis. Rather, it is a manifestation of psychological distress. In a legal or
policy context, the word malingering may be used to indicate the purposeful and conscious
effort to defraud. In general, surgeons should not use this word and leave this determination
to lawyers and judges.

The Biopsychosocial Paradigm of Illness
Many patients being treated for a work injury claim are relatively easy to treat, interested
in their own speedy recovery, and have outcomes similar to patients cared for under
commercial insurance or public insurance. A subset of individuals have underlying
external stressors (eg, financial, home, job, or relationship insecurity), adverse work
dynamics (eg, poor relationship with manager or employer, dispute regarding the work
claim, perception that the employer is at fault), notable levels of distress (symptoms of
depression or anxiety), and unhealthy thoughts/misconceptions (eg, worst-case thinking,
fear of painful movement, inflexible thinking, discomfort with uncertainty). These mental
and social health opportunities account for much of the variation in the intensity and
duration of symptoms and activity intolerance. This is true for patients treated under a
work claim and those treated in other clinical settings.5
Several important misconceptions may contribute to illness, perhaps more so in a work
setting. For example, cognitive biases (systematic errors in thought because of the
mind’s use of shortcuts, known as heuristics), such as post hoc ergo propter hoc (because
of this, therefore this); confirmation bias; and the anchoring heuristic are common
sources of misconceptions (cognitive error) in patients with new symptoms at work and
in the clinicians who treat them.6,7 Evidence shows that gradual onset, age-related
diseases, such as arthritis, tendinopathy, and neuropathy, often are misinterpreted as
new pathology at the time the symptoms are first noticed.8,9 New symptoms of pain
often are misinterpreted as injury (why else would I hurt?). Each state has legal
precedents that determine terms of coverage under work claims that preempt the
science. In other words, some conditions may be covered despite good evidence that
they are definitely not, or probably not, caused by work. The orthopaedic surgeon
should follow the scientific evidence rather than policy in addressing cause, diagnosis,
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:01 AM
AAOS | Workers’ Compensation
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001158
8/26

work-relatedness, management, outcomes, restrictions, capability, and activity
intolerance.
A cross-sectional national survey reported moderate (28%) or severe (14%) psychological
distress among workers’ compensation claimants.10 Among workers reporting a
musculoskeletal disorder and psychological distress, only 27% accessed mental health
services.10 The factor most strongly associated with long-term disability in patients with
low back pain is depression.11 Symptoms of depression are common in the absence of a
diagnosis of major depression. Symptoms of depression or anxiety at any level are
associated with greater pain intensity and greater activity intolerance. Extensive
evidence shows that symptoms of depression or anxiety are associated with suboptimal
self-reported patient outcomes (greater symptom intensity and incapability [activity
intolerance]).5 Workers who file an injury claim also may be more likely to experience
major depression compared with those who sustain a nonoccupational injury or who do
not sustain an injury.12 Symptoms of depression are bidirectional: they may arise from a
severe injury and protracted recovery, and they may also make an injury seem more
severe (greater symptom intensity and activity intolerance).
In the past, incongruity between capacity and activity tolerance may have been
considered as malingering or catching someone in a lie. Although intentional
misrepresentation (such as a patient presenting one manner in the office and another
manner if surveilled unsuspectingly, or if a patient’s social media accounts are
incongruous with their clinical presentation) that is filmed deserves special consideration
and is strong evidence of incongruity, most incongruities can be considered evidence of
mental and social health opportunities. They are part of the illness.
Epidemiology
In 2019, 2.8 million nonfatal work claims were reported among private industry employers.13
In 2018, 272,780 musculoskeletal work claims were filed in the private sector in the United
States, with 96% of these claims ascribed to trauma.14
Soft-tissue diagnoses (sprains and strains) are the most common sources of musculoskeletal
work claims, with an incidence rate of 26 per 10,000 full-time workers in the private sector.14
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:01 AM
AAOS | Workers’ Compensation
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001158
9/26

The annual estimated direct and indirect cost attributable to individuals with a musculoskeletal
disease is $213 billion. Considering all costs for individuals with a musculoskeletal disease,
including other comorbid conditions, the cost of treating these individuals and the cost to
society in the form of decreased wages is estimated to be almost $874 billion a year. Over the
past 15 years, costs associated with musculoskeletal conditions have risen from 3.43% to
5.73% of the gross domestic product.15
Pathophysiology
High-energy trauma may cause fracture or dislocation.
Abnormal tendons (tendinopathy) may rupture with lower levels energy.
Lacerations and penetrating injuries may injure tendons, muscles, nerves, and blood vessels.
Crush and contusion without fracture causes transient pathology in the absence of
compartment syndrome.
The concept of tissue damage related to activity is overstated and potentially harmful.
The concept that activity causes pathophysiology may reinforce misconceptions, such as
worst-case thinking and fear of painful movement. Ideas may cause or worsen illness as
demonstrated in the nocebo effect, mass psychogenic illness, and other manifestations.16,17
Stick to the science
The concept that activity causes pathophysiology is contrary to most scientific evidence.
Exercise is healthy.
Tissues (bones, tendons, ligaments) respond to stress by remodeling and strengthening.
Only unusual stress that the tissue has not already accommodated may cause a problem
(eg, stress fracture).
It is difficult to establish a causal relationship, and evidence that pathophysiology may be
related to activity is inconclusive with uncommon exception (eg, ligament insufficiency and
elbow arthritis in baseball pitchers). Err toward no relationship.
Account for cognitive errors resulting from bias, a key aspect of the normal function of the
human mind.
Cognitive bias may result in misinterpretation of the relationship between symptoms and
activity as a relationship between pathophysiology and activity.
Post hoc ergo propter hoc (I never had symptoms until the event, so the event must have
caused the problem.)
Confirmation bias. We believe there is a relationship, so we perceive one.
SEND FEEDBACK

AAOS | Workers’ Compensation
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001158
10/26

Anchoring bias. It is suggested to us that there is a relationship, and we anchor on that
possibility.
Classification
Definitions Workers’ Compensation Terms
Different jurisdictions may assign somewhat different meanings to the same words.
Commonly accepted words and definitions (not universal)
Impairment: deviation or loss of body structure or of physiologic or psychological function
(objectively measurable)
Disease: a pathologic condition of a body part (objectively measurable pathophysiology)
Illness: the total effect of an injury or disease on the entire person; the subjective state of
being unwell.
Disability: reported inability to perform an activity in the manner or within the range
considered normal for an individual
Disease can cause impairment.
The subjective (illness, disability) often does not correspond with the objective (disease or
impairment).

Definitions Workers’ Compensation Terms
Terminology is important in workers’ compensation claims. It also varies slightly from
state to state. In some cases, the medical and legal definitions of a word or phrase do
not correlate or may seem at odds. Workers’ compensation in the United States is an
administrative; legal; and, in most cases, a state-run process. It relies on the legal rather
than medical definitions of terms, especially if a dispute or contested claim exists.
Consider, for example, the word disabled. If used by a physician, it generally describes
someone who is incapacitated by an illness or injury. A physician may even mean in a
broader sense that “disability is the alteration of a person’s capacity to meet personal,
social, or occupational demands.” However, legally in federal Social Security disability
claims, disabled means unable to pursue any gainful employment based on impairments
and prior training and experience for at least 12 months.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:01 AM
AAOS | Workers’ Compensation
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001158
11/26

The World Health Organization defines disability in a medical sense as “any restriction or
lack of ability to perform an activity in the manner or within the range of considered
normal for a human being.” Any individual who loses a finger by this definition would be
partially disabled; however, the workers’ compensation laws in almost all states suggest
a more legal definition of disability in that a loss of the ability to maintain a wage or
employment exists because of the injury. Therefore, a concert pianist who loses a finger
would be legally disabled for that job, but an office administrator would not be disabled
for his or her job. As an example of a state-level definition, the definition of disability in
the workers’ compensation act in Texas is as follows: “disability means the inability
because of a compensable injury to obtain and retain employment at wages equivalent
to the preinjury wage” (Texas Labor Code §401.011).16
Evaluation
Interview
Document information relayed about the specifics of an event along with the source of that
information.
Note incongruence
Between the patient’s experience of the event and other forms of documentation
Between the symptom intensity and activity intolerance expected based on the identified or
expected pathophysiology and what the patient expresses.
Document other relevant illnesses and their management.
Document prior workers’ compensation claims and prior lawsuits over non–work-related
injuries.
Document a work history.
How long the patient has worked at the job
Prior work experience
Concurrent employment at a second or third job
Job satisfaction
Recent job changes, such as increased workload resulting from layoffs
Conflicts with a supervisor or associates
A high-demand/low-control (stressful) work environment
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:01 AM
AAOS | Workers’ Compensation
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001158
12/26


Interview
Treating clinicians should be attentive to several aspects of care and documentation. All
inconsistencies should be specifically identified and documented. An example is a
patient who reports no prior symptoms but physical examination and diagnostic testing
demonstrate long-standing disease. Although the claimant may have not noticed
symptoms, the problem may not be new. Other inconsistencies, such as symptoms that
are more diffuse than the pathology accounts for, activity intolerance greater than
expected for a given pathology, and variation in features of the interview or examination,
may be present. The symptoms and body parts involved may be different from those
described in the medical records of providers who saw the patient before referral to the
orthopaedist.
The treating surgeon can label these as inconsistencies, or medically unexplainable, but
should avoid saying the worker is not credible because that typically is a judicial decision.
The surgeon’s medical records, especially the history of the present illness (specifically
how and why the injury occurred, preferably in the patient’s own words), are a crucial
and informative source for claims investigation. Compared with records for patients who
are not treated under a work injury claim, more time and more detail usually are
required from the orthopaedic surgeon. Details of what is known objectively (eg, video,
physical examination, tests) and what is reported by the patient regarding position of the
body when injured, the forces that were placed on the body, weights, and direction, are
important to document. Document the source of the information, which often is a direct
report from the patient. For example, if the injury is from a fall, additional detail about
how the patient fell, how far they fell, how they landed, and what they immediately felt
at the time of injury may be important to include in the history of present illness. This
level of detail is required asked to testify about causation; however, this level of detail is
not required for other injuries treated in health insurance. For those, a one-sentence
statement, such as “he slipped in wet grass while picking up small branches after a
storm” is sufficient.

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001158
13/26

Physical Examination
Document objective impairment/pathophysiology.
Document inconsistencies with known or expected pathophysiology.
Document if the examination is limited because of disproportionate symptoms and
protectiveness.
Non-discrete tenderness (diffuse, vague findings)
Disproportionate (unexpected) symptoms or incapacity
Inconsistent findings (eg, foot symptoms with straight leg raise lying down, but not sitting)
Examination findings that change if repeated
Limited effort (eg, initial strength followed by weakness, often referred to as giveaway
weakness).
Can be measured using grip strength at five stations, meaning that the grip size, or distance
between handles, is varied, which should result in greater strength at the second or third
station and an appropriate curve downward at the first, fourth, and fifth stations. A flat
distribution of strength in the absence of pain produced by this test indicates limited effort.
Can be measured by rapidly alternating left and right grip strength with highly variable
values.
Imaging Studies
Strict use of imaging similar to other contexts. In general, imaging is overused and misused.
Ensure greater potential for benefit than for harm exists before ordering a diagnostic test.
Imaging studies rarely are necessary for diagnosis (exception: fracture). Alternatives to
imaging studies if diagnosis is unclear:
Schedule an early specialty care consultation with a thoughtful, discerning specialist.
Diagnose the most likely issue, rule out dangerous issues (along with a specialist consultant
if desired), and monitor over time.
Both of the following should be present before ordering a diagnostic test.
Relatively high-pretest odds of detecting an important and meaningful abnormality. Tests
often are misleading in low-prevalence environments because incidental findings and age-
appropriate changes are overinterpreted and misinterpreted.
An improvement in health that would result from imaging that abnormality. A treatment
option must make the test worthwhile.
Care should be taken to not misinterpret expected age-appropriate changes.18
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:01 AM
AAOS | Workers’ Compensation
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001158
14/26

For example, signal changes associated with rotator cuff tendinopathy and knee arthritis
often are misinterpreted as a tear, thereby reinforcing unhealthy misconceptions.
Consider MRI of both shoulders or both knees if indicated. Currently, this may be possible
only in Texas with an employer who has opted out of workers’ compensation.
Most age-appropriate changes are easily diagnosed without imaging studies. The best
approach is to not get an MRI.
Studies show that ordering a spine MRI early in the course of care of a patient with
absent, objective, substantial neurologic deficit on physical examination results in poorer
outcomes.19-21
Any findings on MRI should be correlated with both symptoms and physical examination
and also should demonstrate pathology distinct from that observed on imaging studies of
asymptomatic individuals at a similar age.
Management
Distinguish necessary (eg, nerve repair) and discretionary treatment options.
Individuals who undergo discretionary surgical treatment under a work claim tend to have
greater final symptom intensity and activity intolerance than individuals who undergo the
same surgical procedure under commercial insurance.22
Similar to care outside a work claim, avoid or strictly limit prescription of opioids. These
medications only are appropriate for a few days postoperatively. See the American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons Pain Alleviation Toolkit for more details.23
Most states adhere to published guidelines for approved management.
The Official Disability Guidelines
American College of Occupational and Environmental Medicine (ACOEM) Occupational
Medicine Practice Guidelines

Management
A systematic review of 20 studies on orthopaedic surgery reported a twofold higher risk
of an unsatisfactory outcome in patients who underwent surgical treatment under a
work claim.22
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:01 AM
AAOS | Workers’ Compensation
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001158
15/26

Most states have guidelines regarding management. In some states. these guidelines are
mandatory, whereas in other states they are strongly recommended. Two popular
nationally recognized guidelines exist. The guidelines used most commonly are the
Official Disability Guidelines, which are published and updated regularly by the Work
Loss Data Institute. The other guidelines are published by American College of
Occupational and Environmental Medicine and known as the Occupational Medicine
Practice Guidelines.
In approximately 35 states, one of these guidelines is required or strongly
recommended. Some states have developed their own supplement to these basic
guidelines (eg, California’s Medical Treatment Utilization Schedule). Varying from the
recommendations in these guidelines regarding management is possible but usually
requires a sound medical decision process. This rationale should be documented in the
clinical notes and be based on evidence that can be referenced or cited. A surgeon’s
professional opinion is important, but it should be founded on the current best medical
evidence. In general, the intention of such guidelines are to reduce the individual
variability in the care of common injuries and protect the patient and other stakeholders
from unnecessary ineffective and potentially harmful medical care.
If a recommend test or treatment a surgeon feels is indicated is denied by another
physician reviewing the patient’s records (called utilization review), the surgeons and the
patient typically have a right to appeal the utilization review decision. Jurisdictions vary
with regard to who decides appeals; however, the more scientific a surgeon’s statement
is with regard to the medical reasons the test or treatment should be authorized
(certified as medically necessary), the more likely the request will be honored on appeal.
The appeal should state if the case is adequately covered by the required treatment
guidelines and the problem is that the medical records failed to record relevant facts or
if the case falls outside the state-adopted guidelines and is an exception to the
guidelines (eg, no evidence-based guidelines are available on the third surgical
procedure for the management of a non-united fracture).
The Medical Record
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:01 AM
AAOS | Workers’ Compensation
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001158
16/26

Work-compensable conditions are listed with an International Classification of Diseases-10
code and distinguished from non-compensable conditions.
Address restrictions and capacity as work guidelines
Complete necessary forms.

The Medical Record
Medical records should include additional information that is not typical for patients
treated outside a workers’ compensation claim. For example, for every office visit, the
work-compensable conditions should be listed with an International Classification of
Diseases-10 code. These should be distinguished from non-compensable conditions. In
addition, restrictions for the employee’s safe return to work must be addressed. Some
states have administrative forms that must be filled out and signed by the treating
physician. The documents confirm the surgeon’s approval that the diagnosis represents
a new work-related and traumatic pathology (an injury), expertise regarding whether
work activity will be harmful and cause worsening of the pathology, and
accommodations that the employer must provide so the employee can safely return to
his or her job.
Return to Work
Being off work for a prolonged period is associated with greater illness and earlier death.24
Early and safe return to duty is best for the employee, the employer, and the insurance
company.
Minimizes illness and illness behavior
Restores role
Improves the self-respect and positive feedback associated with knowing one is valued by
society
Creates camaraderie and teamwork with associates
Minimizes deconditioning and development of unhealthy habits
An unpleasant, stressful work environment greatly reduces the likelihood that an injured
worker will return to work.

Employer factors and early return to work
The employer should support injured workers.
Accommodate workers with any restrictions or incapacity.
Retrain or reassign workers with temporary or permanent incapacities.
Employer or fellow employee hostility intensifies worker stress.
Some employers use injury or disability as a method to dismiss workers.
Worker factors and return to work
Care under a work claim is associated with prolonged and less complete recovery compared
with individuals who have similar conditions managed under other forms of insurance.
Union rules occasionally do not allow injured workers to be assigned to lighter jobs if other
available workers have more seniority.

Return to Work
In 1997, the Canadian Medical Association published “The Physician’s Role in Helping
Patients Return to Work After Illness or Injury.” The association stated that “prolonged
absence from one’s normal roles, including absence from the workplace is detrimental
to a person’s mental, physical and social well-being.”25 Therefore, physicians should
encourage a patient’s return to function and work as soon as possible.” In the United
States, this concept was reiterated in policy statements from the American College of
Occupational and Environmental Medicine in 2006, the American Medical Association in
2004, and the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons in 2000. Return to work
improves the injury outcome and prevents the known decline in overall health and
longevity that occurs in individuals who are out of work for a prolonged period. Return to
work limits deconditioning and psychological sequelae.
Causation
Cause is variably defined by each state.
In some jurisdictions, causation must be more than one-half the reason for the condition or
its need for management (primary cause or predominant cause).

In other jurisdictions, the work exposure only needs to be a cause, even if it makes a small
potential contribution to the total pathology.
Orthopaedic surgeons just describe the interview, physical examination, and pathology.
Causation decisions are policy decisions made by other individuals.
Major trauma requires almost no causation analysis.
Examples: falls from roofs, high-speed motor vehicle collisions, and traumatic amputations.
New symptoms from pathology consistent with the worker’s age or from prior health history
(eg, prior rotator cuff surgery) must be distinguished from new pathology related to a
traumatic event.9,18,26
This typically is apparent on physical examination, with no benefit from imaging studies.
For example, crepitus in the knee indicates arthritis, and surgeons can anticipate that
radiographs and MRIs would be consistent, including degenerative meniscal lesions that
radiologists tend to label as tears, which inappropriately implies injury.
Rotator cuff tendinopathy without a large defect also can be diagnosed on physical
examination. Physical examination findings consistent with a traumatic defect (eg, loss of
active motion and/or strength [more than just limited effort or pain avoidance]) may
merit imaging studies. Small degenerative defects and signal changes also often are
labeled by radiologists as tears (rather than thinning), which inappropriately implies
injury. Larger defects associated with rotator cuff muscle atrophy and fatty infiltration are
clearly long-standing pathology rather than an acute rupture.
Claims based on daily work activity rather than a single traumatic event merit special
consideration because the concept of tissue damage from use is debatable in most contexts.
Document the tasks and forces, the number of daily repetitions of specific tasks, and the
number of months or years the employee has performed the particular job.

Causation
Many physician opinions and judicial decisions have not been based on the best
available scientific evidence but were founded on a popular opinion or speculation in the
past or on information published in the lay press. Carpal tunnel syndrome is exemplary.
Medical evidence supports that the condition is largely genetic, perhaps multifactorial,
and unlikely directly related to work exposure.27 Yet carpal tunnel syndrome often is

considered work compensable. This difference is frustrating and often results in
dissatisfaction of litigants, judges, and other parties involved.
Clinicians must separate the distinct concepts of medical and legal causation. Medical
causation is determined based on science. Legal causation stems from a desire for social
justice. Medical causation accumulates and evolves over time based on experimental
evidence. Legal causation takes expert medical opinions as if they were established facts
and considers them evidence. Legal causation also may be influenced by policy and
precedent. For these and other reasons, medical and legal causation analyses may reach
different conclusions.
Clinicians and scientists should distinguish a true causal relationship from a correlation.
For example, people with gray hair have a higher incidence of myocardial infarction;
however, having gray-haired is not a biologically plausible explanation for a heart attack.
These are referenced as causal fallacies in the AMA Guides to the Evaluation of Disease and
Injury Causation.2 Legally, the phrase post hoc ergo propter hoc is descriptive of this type
of reasoning.
To better illustrate this concept, consider the following statements. “It never was before,
but it is now, so it must be because of that.” “The rooster crows, and then the sun rises
[perfect temporal correlation], but the rooster itself does not make the sun rise.” “I never
hurt before and now I hurt, so it must be cause and effect” is similarly false reasoning
but may be accepted as evidence of causation in some jurisdictions. The scientific
approach to causation examines the degree to which a concept is supported by evidence
for each of the Bradford Hill criteria.27
Proximate cause is a legal term meaning a consideration of all the facts in a specific case
legally establishes causation. Physicians should not use this term and should decline to
answer any question in testimony or records that asks for a medical opinion on
proximate cause. Proximate cause is a decision for the judge or jury (also known as the
trier of fact).

Apportionment
Apportionment is separation of permanent impairment from a work injury from permanent
impairment from other cause (disease, age, nonwork injury).
Apportionment also may involve separating the amount of pathology from the current work
injury and prior work injuries.
Maximum Medical Improvement
General definition: the earlier of one of the following:
The point at which meaningful improvement in pathophysiology (eg, healing of a fracture) is
no longer anticipated
A time limit set by state policy.
If the patient reaches maximum medical improvement (MMI), he or she is eligible for an
impairment rating, which results in an assignment of benefits.

Maximum Medical Improvement
Healed does not necessarily mean back to the worker’s normal condition of life before
the injury. Injuries may result in lifelong impairment (eg, amputations, lumbar burst
fractures), and residual pathology may merit additional medical care for many years. The
surgeon can determine if the patient is as good as he or she is going to get with the
available medical care, termed MMI.
For example, a patient recovering from volar plate fixation of a fracture of the distal
radius will have a healed bone and most motion back within 3 to 6 months postinjury.
Although slight improvements in comfort and mobility are expected for as long as 1 year,
these improvements will be relatively small in magnitude and MMI can be designated.
As another example, consider a knee contusion in a patient with an arthritic knee. The
pathophysiology associated with the contusion largely is resolved 1 to 3 months
postinjury, depending on the severity of the contusion. Pain from the underlying arthritis
does not constitute an injury. Surgeons must distinguish these two and assign MMI after
an appropriate interval for the contusion, even if the patient still feels limited by

therapy even though no improvement is occurring. Surgeons should rely on evidence to
support science-based decisions.
Permanent Partial Impairment
Workers are compensated for permanent impairment resulting from a work injury.
Examples: loss of limb, loss of motion in a joint, loss of sensibility from nerve injury
Each state has different rules about who may perform impairment ratings.
The assessment must be based on medical probability, also known as medical certainty, which
implies that a statement or opinion is correct with more than 50% certainty.
In 38 states, providing a medically probable opinion about an injured worker’s impairment
generally requires using the AMA Guides to the Evaluation of Permanent Impairment (third,
fourth, fifth, or sixth edition, depending on the state).28
This reference provides tables and other standardized methods (depending on the body part
or parts involved) for determining impairment.
Impairments are translated into disability ratings by state workers’ compensation boards and
judges.

Permanent Partial Impairment
The patient is compensated monetarily for the permanent pathophysiology he or she
has incurred as a result of the work injury. Examples may include loss of a limb or
permanent loss of sensation in part of a limb or loss of motion in a joint. This assignment
of benefits is another aspect of the indemnity program. Surgeons may have to offer their

carrier and the injured employee can factor that into the settlement. Some states do not
require this because all future medical care is covered by the carrier for life given it is
deemed related to the work event. This usually is a function of the state in which the
injury occurred or the state in which the policy was issued.
This is an important aspect of the life of the claim. In some states, it is referred to as
claim closure. In some states, claim closure occurs with a one-time settlement to the
injured employee. In other states, claim closure may be signified by the end of active
medical management, allowing future medical care if deemed necessary. In other states,
claims are closed on a predetermined date from the date of injury regardless of what is
occurring medically. Claim closure is an important milestone in every claim. Ultimately,
the success of the workers’ compensation claim process depends on orthopaedic
surgeons’ attentiveness to their responsibilities and participation in the process.
